title: The Sleeping Lighthouse
summary: When the old lighthouse goes dark for the first time in a hundred years, Nina discovers it never guided ships at all — it kept something out.

chapters.title: The Light That Never Slept
chapters.body:
The lighthouse of Bitter Rock had a single rule, and everyone in Oystershell knew it by heart: the light could never, ever go out. Not during the storm that tore off the rooftops the winter Nina's grandfather was young. Not on the night the sea rose so high that fish swam down the main street. The light had turned up there for a hundred years, red as an ember seen from afar, and people slept soundly because it was lit.

Nina lived at the foot of the lighthouse with her grandmother, who was the keeper. Keeper was a serious title, passed from hand to hand like a ring too heavy for the finger. Her grandmother climbed the one hundred and thirty-seven steps every night, lit the wick, cleaned the glass with a rag that smelled of salt and of something old, and came down only when the sun rose. Nina thought all of it was old-fashioned. There were electric lamps in the world. There were boats with engines that could see in the dark on their own.

"Why do we still do it the hard way?" Nina asked, one night, while her grandmother wound her scarf up to her chin.

Her grandmother stopped in the doorway. The lamplight made her shadow stretch up the wall until it touched the ceiling.

"Because the light isn't for outside," she said. "It's for inside."

Nina didn't understand, and her grandmother didn't explain. Keepers were like that: they spoke in riddles and then climbed stairs.

That night, something different happened. Nina woke in absolute darkness. Not the ordinary dark, full of grey shapes and the glow of the street. A thick dark, bottomless, as if someone had poured black ink into the room and drowned everything. It took her a frightening while to understand what was wrong.

The red light no longer came through the gap in the curtain.

The lighthouse had gone dark.

Nina sat up in bed with her heart pounding in her ears. Outside, the wind had stopped. The sea, which had roared day and night her whole life, was silent — and the silence was worse than any roar. It was the silence of something large holding its breath.

"Gran?" she called.

No one answered.

She climbed out of bed. The stone floor was cold as the bottom of a well. She felt her way to her grandmother's door and pushed it open. The bed was empty, the blankets thrown back, the scarf hanging on its hook. Her grandmother had not gone up. Her grandmother was gone.

In the cracked mirror in the hallway, as Nina passed, she swore she saw something that was not her reflection — something long and pale that watched her from inside the glass and smiled slowly, like someone who has waited a long time and knows the waiting is over. When she turned to look straight at it, it was only the mirror, and her own face, white with fear.

High above, at the top of the lighthouse, a door slammed on its own.

Nina swallowed hard. She could wake the town. She could run, shout, pound on doors. But the sea was silent and her grandmother was up there, in the dark, and something in that silence said there was no time. That every minute without the light was an invitation.

She took the lamp, lit it with trembling hands, and set her foot on the first of the one hundred and thirty-seven steps.

The lamp's flame leaned backward, as if something above were pulling the air into itself.

chapters.title: One Hundred and Thirty-Seven Steps
chapters.body:
Climbing the lighthouse by day was tiring enough. At night, in the dark, with a lamp that made the shadows dance like people, it was another thing entirely. Nina counted the steps under her breath so she wouldn't have to hear the silence. Twenty. Twenty-one. The staircase spiraled up the curved wall, and at each turn there was a narrow little window. Through them, Nina saw the sea far below — smooth, black, still as a lake of tar. No waves. No foam. A surface waiting.

At the fortieth step, she began to hear the voice.

It was low and came from the walls, or from inside them. It didn't shout. It whispered, the way an adult whispers to a child he means to trick — all sweetness on the outside and hunger within.

"Niiina," said the voice. "Open the door up top, Nina. Your grandmother is cold. She's waiting for me. Come open it so she can go out."

Nina gripped the railing. The voice knew her name. The voice knew about her grandmother. But her grandmother had taught her something, long before this night, without seeming to teach anything at all: when a voice you don't know knows too much about you, it is not on your side.

"You're not my grandmother," Nina said, and her own voice came out steadier than she expected.

The whisper laughed. The laugh ran down the stairs like cold water.

"Clever. The old woman was clever too. A hundred years she held me here behind the glass. A hundred years lighting the flame so I couldn't pass. But she grew tired, Nina. Every keeper grows tired. And when they tire, the light goes out, and I wake."

Nina kept climbing. Seventy. Seventy-one. Her hands ached from gripping the lamp, because as long as the flame stayed lit, the whisper kept its distance. She understood, then, her grandmother's riddle. The light isn't for outside. It's for inside. The lighthouse had never guided a single boat. Boats had their own instruments, their own engines. The lighthouse of Bitter Rock was a lock. And the red light, turning year after year, was the key turning in the lock, keeping outside — or inside the glass — the long, pale thing that now whispered her name.

On the hundredth step, she found her grandmother's shoe. Just one, fallen on its side, still warm.

"She ran up," said the whisper, closer now, coming from above. "Running to stop me. Too late. The flame went out on its own, Nina. Too old. Too tired. Just like your little lamp will, any moment now."

Nina looked at the flame. It had grown smaller. The oil in the lamp was running out.

Fear rose in her throat like water on the tide. For an instant — just one — she thought of dropping everything, going back down the hundred steps, running out into the night and never coming back. Letting the town sleep on, none the wiser. Letting the black sea do whatever the black sea wanted.

But then she thought of her grandmother, up there, with one shoe gone, in the dark, having climbed one hundred and thirty-seven steps on old legs just to try to light a flame before it was too late. Her grandmother had not run away from the danger. She had run into it.

Keepers were like that.

Nina took a deep breath, cupped her hand around the dwindling flame, and climbed the last of the steps. At the top, the door of the light room stood ajar, and through it leaked not brightness but a cold that fogged the glass of the lamp. Inside, something long and pale was bent over a small shape curled on the floor, and the small shape was her grandmother.

Nina pushed the door open.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gives Back
chapters.body:
The light room was round, all of glass, and at its center stood the great lens of the lighthouse — a flower of crystal as tall as Nina, dark now, without flame. Bent before it was the thing. Up close it was not a monster of teeth and claws. It was worse: it was almost human. Too long, too pale, with fingers that reached too far and a smile that went from ear to ear on a face that seemed to remember how to be a person, but to have forgotten the details.

Her grandmother lay at the foot of the lens, breathing, but with her eyes closed. The thing raised its head slowly when Nina came in, and its smile stretched wider still.

"The little granddaughter," it said, its voice now coming from its mouth, not the walls. "You've brought me a light. How kind."

Nina's lamp flickered. There was oil enough for a minute, perhaps less. She looked from the dying flame to the great dark lens, and she understood what she needed to do, and she understood that it was nearly impossible, and she did it anyway.

There was no use fighting that thing. It was made of dark, and you don't beat the dark by hitting it. You beat the dark by lighting a light.

Nina ran — not away from the thing, but past it, to the base of the great lens, where the old wick sat that her grandmother lit every night. The thing spun, quick as an eel, and one of its long, cold fingers closed around Nina's ankle. The cold climbed her leg like ice inside the bone. She fell. The lamp flew from her hand, rolled across the glass floor, and the flame nearly went out in the jolt.

Nearly.

Nina stretched out her whole arm, her fingers scraping the floor, the cold of the thing rising to her knee, and reached the lamp at the very instant the flame was only a blue point the size of a seed. She touched that blue point to the old wick of the great lens — the wick soaked in a hundred years of oil, of salt, and of the stubbornness of keepers.

The wick caught.

The light burst outward, not like a candle, but like a sunrise. Red, enormous, alive, it filled the round glass room and passed through the long, pale thing from one side to the other. The thing did not scream. It did something worse: it came apart, like smoke the wind finds, retreating into the dark glass of the window, into the reflection, into the place between what is real and what only lurks. The cold finger let go of Nina's ankle. The cold drained from her leg slowly, like an ebbing tide.

And the lens began to turn. On its own. Slowly at first, then in the old, sure rhythm, throwing the red light out to sea in wide, patient sweeps. Far below, as if it had been given permission, the sea breathed again: one wave, then another, then the old roar, the good old roar that rocked the town to sleep.

Her grandmother opened her eyes. She saw Nina at the foot of the lit lens, trembling, with only one shoe — because somewhere along the way she had lost hers too — and she smiled a tired, proud smile.

"You lit it," said her grandmother.

"I lit it," said Nina.

"Then now you know." Her grandmother held out her hand, and Nina helped her up. "The light isn't for outside, child. It's for inside. And every keeper, one night, learns why we never let it go out."

They went down together, the one hundred and thirty-seven steps, in no hurry, while behind and above them the old red light turned, and turned, and turned — awake, and willing to stay that way for another hundred years.
